items.stem: Damage to Broca's area typically causes which problem?
items.answer: Difficulty producing fluent speech
items.markingKey: B. Broca's aphasia: slow, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension.

items.stem: Explain what the study by Sperry (1968) suggests about lateralisation of language in the left hemisphere.
items.answer: Findings: objects shown to the right visual field (left hemisphere) could be named, while objects shown to the left visual field (right hemisphere) could not be named but could be selected with the left hand. Link: these results are evidence about lateralisation of language in the left hemisphere.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for accurate findings (objects shown to the right visual field (left hemisphere) could be named, while objects shown to the left visual field (right hemisphere) could not be named but could be selected with the left hand); remaining marks for explicitly explaining what the findings show about lateralisation of language in the left hemisphere (not just restating them).

items.stem: Outline the findings of Broca (1861) and explain one conclusion about localisation of speech production that can be drawn from them.
items.answer: Findings: Leborgne had a lesion in the left inferior frontal lobe; similar lesions were found in other patients with speech production problems. Link: these results are evidence about localisation of speech production.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for accurate findings (Leborgne had a lesion in the left inferior frontal lobe; similar lesions were found in other patients with speech production problems); remaining marks for explicitly explaining what the findings show about localisation of speech production (not just restating them).

items.stem: Describe the study by Sperry (1968) and explain what it shows about lateralisation of language in the left hemisphere.
items.answer: Sperry (1968). Aim: to investigate the functions of the two hemispheres when the corpus callosum has been cut. Method: Patients whose corpus callosum had been severed to treat epilepsy were shown images briefly to one visual field and asked to name or select objects with one hand. Findings: objects shown to the right visual field (left hemisphere) could be named, while objects shown to the left visual field (right hemisphere) could not be named but could be selected with the left hand Link: lateralisation of language in the left hemisphere.

items.stem: With reference to a patient after a left-hemisphere stroke, explain how it illustrates localisation of language.
items.answer: Kenji, 62, from Hanoi, has a stroke in the left frontal lobe; he understands what people say but struggles to produce words. His symptoms match Broca's aphasia, supporting the view that speech production is localised in the left inferior frontal lobe
items.markingKey: Context (Kenji, 62, from Hanoi, has a stroke in the left frontal lobe; he understands what people say but struggles to produce words.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: his symptoms match Broca's aphasia, supporting the view that speech production is localised in the left inferior frontal lobe – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to localisation of language.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Brain imaging technology has shown that behaviour can be explained by localised brain functions."
items.answer: Imaging supports a degree of localisation, but behaviour is better explained by interacting networks than by single areas.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: fMRI and lesion studies identify specialised areas (Broca, fusiform face area); split-brain studies show lateralisation (Sperry, 1968). Arguments against: activity is distributed across networks; imaging is correlational and interpretation is subjective; plasticity allows reorganisation. Supported judgement: Imaging supports a degree of localisation, but behaviour is better explained by interacting networks than by single areas.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "PET"?
options: The reabsorption of a neurotransmitter by the presynaptic neuron after it has been released
Positron emission tomography: imaging of brain activity by detecting a radioactive tracer, such as labelled glucose, taken up by active areas
A chemical that increases the action of a neurotransmitter, e.g. by mimicking it or blocking its reuptake
The reorganisation of the cortex so that an area takes over a function previously served by another area, e.g. after injury
items.answer: Positron emission tomography: imaging of brain activity by detecting a radioactive tracer, such as labelled glucose, taken up by active areas
items.markingKey: B. "PET" is positron emission tomography: imaging of brain activity by detecting a radioactive tracer, such as labelled glucose, taken up by active areas.

items.stem: Explain the difference between Wernicke's area and Broca's area.
items.answer: Broca's area (left frontal lobe) is associated with speech production, while Wernicke's area (left temporal lobe) is associated with understanding language.
items.markingKey: Broca's area (left frontal lobe) is associated with speech production, while Wernicke's area (left temporal lobe) is associated with understanding language. items.stem: Describe the study by Broca (1861) and explain what it shows about localisation of speech production.
items.answer: Broca (1861). Aim: to identify the brain area associated with loss of speech. Method: Broca examined a patient, Leborgne, who could understand speech but could only say "tan"; after his death a post-mortem examination of the brain was carried out. Findings: Leborgne had a lesion in the left inferior frontal lobe; similar lesions were found in other patients with speech production problems Link: localisation of speech production.

items.stem: A 70-year-old in Lisbon starts learning Mandarin. Using neuroplasticity, explain why this might benefit her brain.
items.answer: Learning new skills forms and strengthens neural networks through LTP and dendritic branching; adult brains remain plastic (Draganski et al., 2004), and cognitively demanding activity may build cognitive reserve.

items.stem: Distinguish between excitatory neurotransmitters and inhibitory neurotransmitters.

items.stem: Describe the study by Antonova et al. (2011) and explain what it shows about the role of acetylcholine in memory formation.
items.answer: Antonova et al. (2011). Aim: to investigate the role of acetylcholine in the encoding of spatial memories. Findings: scopolamine reduced hippocampal activation during the encoding of spatial memories compared with placebo Link: the role of acetylcholine in memory formation.

items.stem: Briefly describe Harlow's rhesus monkeys and explain what it reveals about the value and ethics of animal research.

items.stem: Using Draganski et al. (2004) as supporting evidence, explain experience-dependent neuroplasticity in the adult brain.
items.answer: Draganski et al. (2004). Aim: to investigate whether learning a new motor skill changes brain structure in adults. Method: 24 volunteers with no juggling experience were scanned and randomly divided into jugglers (who learned a three-ball cascade over three months) and non-jugglers; scans were repeated after three months of practice and after three months without practice. Findings: jugglers showed increased grey matter in the mid-temporal area (hMT/V5) and left posterior intraparietal sulcus; this decreased again after they stopped juggling Link: experience-dependent neuroplasticity in the adult brain.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: jugglers showed increased grey matter in the mid-temporal area (hMT/V5) and left posterior intraparietal sulcus; this decreased again after they stopped juggling); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to experience-dependent neuroplasticity in the adult brain. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: Using Sperry (1968) as supporting evidence, explain lateralisation of language in the left hemisphere.
items.answer: Sperry (1968). Aim: to investigate the functions of the two hemispheres when the corpus callosum has been cut. Method: Patients whose corpus callosum had been severed to treat epilepsy were shown images briefly to one visual field and asked to name or select objects with one hand. Findings: objects shown to the right visual field (left hemisphere) could be named, while objects shown to the left visual field (right hemisphere) could not be named but could be selected with the left hand Link: lateralisation of language in the left hemisphere.

items.stem: With reference to Olds and Milner (1954), explain how research has investigated the discovery of a brain reward system.
items.answer: Olds and Milner (1954). Aim: to investigate whether stimulation of particular brain areas could act as a reward. Method: Electrodes were implanted in different brain areas of rats, which could press a lever to deliver a small electrical stimulation to their own brain. Findings: rats with electrodes in the septal area pressed the lever at high rates - up to thousands of times per hour - suggesting the brain has a reward system Link: the discovery of a brain reward system.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The brain is shaped more by experience than by genes."
items.answer: Genes set the basic architecture, but experience continually reshapes networks; both interact.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: plasticity research (Maguire et al., 2000; Draganski et al., 2004); enriched environments change cortical thickness (Rosenzweig et al., 1972). Arguments against: basic brain structure is genetically programmed; genes influence plasticity itself; correlational evidence in humans. Supported judgement: Genes set the basic architecture, but experience continually reshapes networks; both interact.

items.stem: Explain the difference between replacement and refinement.
items.answer: Replacement means using alternatives to animals altogether (e.g. computer modelling), while refinement means improving procedures so animals that are used suffer as little as possible.

items.stem: Briefly explain why brain imaging research cannot always show that a brain area causes a behaviour.
items.answer: Imaging shows correlation between activity (or structure) and behaviour; the area may be active because of the task without being necessary for it, and the direction of causality is unclear - lesion or stimulation studies are needed for stronger causal claims.
